summary: Describes a proposal for long-term Internet addressing, routing and scaling by running TCP and UDP over larger addresses, using the CLNP network layer. It is a historic informational paper from the debate over replacing IPv4.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1347 proposes keeping TCP and UDP while replacing IP with CLNP, which can use larger network addresses. It describes a gradual migration in which updated hosts and routers can continue to communicate with older IP systems.

questions: tcp and udp with bigger addresses

subtitle: A proposal to run TCP and UDP over CLNP with larger network addresses.

tldr.problem: RFC 1347 describes concerns that the 32-bit IP address space and rapidly growing routing information could limit Internet growth. Any change needed to allow incremental deployment without interrupting existing service.
tldr.mechanism: TUBA proposes updating hosts to carry TCP and UDP over CLNP, using larger NSAP addresses, and updating DNS and routers so old and updated hosts can communicate during a gradual transition.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an informational overview of a proposal and leaves detailed operation for further study. The unit metadata classifies it as Historic.

today: RFC 1347 is an Informational proposal from June 1992, and the unit metadata classifies it as Historic. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Addressing and Routing Problem
sections.content:
The memo says that the Internet faced growing routing information and a shortage of IP network numbers. It estimates that routing information was growing at approximately twice its size each year and argues for a system that could scale while allowing a gradual transition.

TUBA means TCP and UDP with Bigger Addresses. The proposal keeps Internet applications and transport protocols while moving the network layer from IP to the Connectionless Network Protocol (CLNP).
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal responds to concerns about IP address capacity and routing growth. It aims to change the network layer without replacing TCP, UDP, or Internet applications.

sections.title: The Proposed Long-Term Design
sections.content:
The memo proposes using CLNP, which it describes as a datagram protocol similar to IP with flexible addresses. Internet applications would continue to use TCP or UDP, but the network layer would carry those protocols over CLNP using Network Service Access Point (NSAP) addresses.

TUBA does not propose a general move to all OSI protocols. It focuses on replacing IP with CLNP and leaves detailed specifications for TCP and UDP operation over CLNP and for a CLNP profile to further study.
sections.plainLanguage: In the proposed design, TCP and UDP stay in place while CLNP carries their packets. The proposal does not require other OSI protocols to replace Internet applications.

sections.title: Communication During Migration
sections.content:
Updated hosts use the existing IP suite to communicate with older hosts and TCP or UDP over CLNP to communicate with other updated hosts. The address returned by a name lookup indicates which network protocol to use. Routers in a domain must forward both IP and CLNP, either through routers that support both or through separate router sets.

The RFC proposes a new DNS record called long-address for NSAP addresses and a reverse record called long-in-addr.arpa. Updated hosts request the long address first and fall back to the regular IP address if it is unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: An updated host uses the address it finds to decide whether to send a packet over IP or CLNP. During the transition, it can still use IP addresses to reach older hosts.

sections.title: Carrying TCP and UDP over CLNP
sections.content:
The proposal places a TCP packet directly inside a CLNP packet, with the TCP header following the CLNP header. UDP is carried in the same way. The RFC identifies the transport checksum pseudo-header as an issue because it was defined in terms of IP addresses and fields.

The memo offers possible ways to construct a pseudo-header for CLNP but does not select a final format. It states that the details are for further study. It also says that the document does not discuss security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP and UDP packets would be carried directly inside CLNP packets. The RFC leaves the exact checksum pseudo-header design unresolved.
